Best way to tell if a game is a JRPG is to look for the super-weapon.

1) Cohesive Art Style. If it's terrible to look at, I tend to be more critical of other things. It doesn't need to look like a AAA title, either. 1990s JRPGs are still played today, because they're fantastic to look at.

2) Interface. As a turn-based RPG, you live and die by how effective/sane your interface is. This is your gameplay section.

3) Characters. We need to care about the characters, both villain, hero, and NPC. Cutscenes are a must. In-game is much preferred! Pausable/skippable is a bonus, especially if a boss fight immediately follows them.

Balance in RPGs...

It is what can make or break a game before it takes off. If there is a broken character then there is no point in playing anything but it. Having well balanced and customizable characters to fit my playstyle is huge.

Secondly a good story line. Give me a reason to get into the game. Flaws in the characters make for realistic individuals. Evil opponents makes me root for the hero. Etc.

The attacks in a turn based RPG have to actually mean something. The effects like bleeding, poison, attack power down, stuff like that, should mean something. If I'm able to power my way through a game ignoring attack types, effects, and basically anything other than my base damage, then the game is boring. There's no reason for me to not just watch a let's play for the story and move along. There needs to be actual repercussions to an enemy using an attack that my character is weak to, or using an effect, other than just a loss on my health bar. It's why Pokemon is so beloved. When a water attack is used against a fire type, the result is catastrophic. When a water attack is used against a ground type, the results are extremely minimal. It's that extra dimension of strategy that makes the simple mechanic of take a turn, give a turn fun.

Beyond that, there should be other things to do in the game other than just the story line, I feel. Genuinely interesting side quests, minigames, and this is just my feelings, but I prefer a game with a certain amount of control over the abilities of the characters, whether I'm controlling a party, or there is a single protagonist. This is, of course, on top of an inventory system that isn't garbage (may even be fun to manage if you're good), loot drops that actually do something for you (a recent example I can think of where I really liked what was dropped in a turn based game is Dragon Fin Soup-- it at least felt like a truly random expereince, and everything you get has an effect on your character), and a solid storyline.

The main thing I look for in a turn based RPG is simplicity. I don't like the "tactical" style RPG combat a la Final Fantasy Tactics. Put my dudes and the bad dudes on the screen at let me beat on them, none of this worrying about what terrain tile I'm on, what direction I'm attacking from, if I have a high ground advantage etc just slap me and the bad dudes on a battle screen and let me do the work from there. About the most "tactical" battle I can stand are the FF6 "control 3 teams and beat up the monsters" type scenario like the lead up to the first battle with Kefka in Narshe. If I wanted a complex calculated approach to every engagement, I'd just fire up Dark Souls, not a turn based RPG.

Flexibility is a must, as well. I don't like when games introduce a cavalcade of characters and you end up with a set party that you have no control over at endgame - this is the reason FFIV Advance is and likely will remain my favorite port of a classic game because it gave you the ability to use all the cool characters you encountered as part of your party throughout the game once you got to the endgame. See also FFVI for this. FFX I think did this really well too with the dynamic party changing in battles.

Being able to see and manipulate the turn order (a la FFX) would be great in a turn based RPG, too.

Let me control my entire party. Looking at you, FFXII.

I hate feeling like I'm being punished for playing the game "wrong". Every option available to me should be just as valid as any other, without making my choice feel meaningless. Little things like choosing to do double damage over attacking twice as fast. At first glance, these do the same things, but it opens up some interesting choices. If I do double damage, there's a good chance I can wipe out one of the little guys in a single hit and allow my party to focus down someone else, or my party could set up an opening that I can exploit best in one solid move. On the other hand, speed would allow me to stack buffs/debuffs much sooner, or try out a few tactics out at once to see which one works best. This allows me to make my character unique without being punished for not having an "optimal build".

This is hard to do as nearly every stat and mechanic in the game needs to work with every other stat and mechanic, and the problem increases exponentially as new features are added (using previous example, 2 attacks mean 2 criticals, but does double damage mean double criticals? Is defense a chance to dodge, percent damage reduction, or flat damage reduction?).

The choices don't even need to be permanent; a battle-by-battle basis would work wonders. Should my mage use a strength or speed spell on my brute in this battle? Should I risk a turn of healing/neglect another teammate to do both? This strengthens the team as a whole and really gets you attached to the characters.

This extends beyond combat, too. Everybody has a very complex and important role, so losing any character is a big deal. Some new guy might fill "the role" of my mage, archer, or warrior, but those subtle differences are going to show. Learning how to cope with the loss of a teammate and trying to get the new guy to fit in while the characters are going through the same thing brings the game to a new level. I don't need to sympathize with the characters when I can empathize with them.

Branching storylines are always a lot of fun.

Next, I'd go for possibilities. Both with character leveling, along with the setting and plot in general. I want the ability to create whatever crazy motherfucker I want, because in the real world you aren't limited by "class-sets" anywhere near as much as you are in games. If a game doesn't have some sort of a "spellsword" class and just has a bunch of squishy mages or something like that, it isn't even remotely realistic. A good example of a game with "open" classes is Final Fantasy Tactics, which allowed you to pretty much mush whatever two classes you wanted together, which gave the game much more variation. Being able to build up a small army like in FFT also helps, but isn't needed. And on a similar note, variation in story. Strategy is intertwined with the so called "butterfly effect", where every action, no matter how small, can have a huge impact. Different playthroughs should result in different endings, such as in Lodis and the Fallout games, though it is certainly more profound in New Vegas.

Finally, overall meaning. Not just for rpgs, but for all games.Pretty much all the games I listed are pretty good with this. Fire Emblem being an examination on evil and the nature of war, Knight of Lodis on humankind's relation to god, along with actions having unforseen results (hard to get into that one without giving away the plot, and most people I know haven't played it yet). It doesn't have to be huge, FFT had a small little critique on escapism which wasn't a big deal, but it was nice to have included. Even Fallout NV was an allegory on the Middle East. Video games are art, that is why initially, they were able to avoid most of this PC censorship bullshit. I feel it is integral to have some depth if something is to be considered a great game.
